title: Carnival of Souls

evidence.note: Wikipedia reports that the US theatrical release failed to include a valid copyright notice on the prints, which would put it in the US public domain. It also reports that the foreign release carried a copyright card and was protected for overseas sales. No primary record (Copyright Office catalog or Catalog of Copyright Entries) was fetched, so the layer is held at undetermined.

The Internet Archive item CarnivalofSouls (runtime 01:22:59) lists creator Herk Harvey, year 1962, and carries a Creative Commons public-domain license URL. This is the uploader's tag, not a rights determination.

Wikipedia credits Gene Moore with the film's original organ score. A score recorded on the film's own track would normally share the print's status, which is itself unconfirmed by a primary record. No separate registration or renewal was checked. A separately released soundtrack recording would be a different work.
John Clifford wrote the screenplay. No pre-existing underlying work was identified, but no primary record was checked.

No active mark was identified, but no trademark database was searched. The 1998 remake (Wes Craven Presents Carnival of Souls) came after producer Peter Soby negotiated remake rights from Herk Harvey and John Clifford. It is a separate work.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright. Slavish copying of public-domain works without originality is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., 36 F. Supp. 2d 191, S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration adds, such as a newly composed or recorded score, new titles or subtitles, commentary or other original material, can be protected. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.

The Criterion Collection issued a 2-disc DVD set in 2000 with a 78-minute theatrical version and an 84-minute director's cut, then a 2016 DVD and Blu-ray reissue with a new restoration. Any added commentary, subtitles or other original material on those discs may be protected.

editorial:
Carnival of Souls was made for about $33,000, shot in Douglas County, Kansas and Salt Lake City, Utah. Herk Harvey directed it, his only feature, from a John Clifford screenplay, with Gene Moore's organ score and Maurice Prather's cinematography. It opened on September 26, 1962, with Herts-Lion International as distributor, on a double bill with The Devil's Messenger. A reuser wants it because Wikipedia reports that the US prints lacked a valid copyright notice, which would put the US release in the public domain, and the Internet Archive hosts a copy tagged with a public-domain license.

The trap is that this status rests on a secondary source. Wikipedia also reports that the foreign release carried a copyright card and was protected for overseas sales. This dossier did not check the Copyright Office catalog or the Catalog of Copyright Entries, so print, score, story and trademark all stay undetermined. Criterion's 2000 DVD set and its 2016 restoration may carry protectable additions, and ripping a copy-protected disc can raise a DMCA issue. The Internet Archive copy is the safer source to use.
faq: Can I upload or reuse Carnival of Souls?

The US release is reported to have lacked a valid copyright notice on its prints, but no primary record was checked here, so treat the status as unconfirmed. The foreign release is reported to have carried a copyright card. The Internet Archive copy is the safest source. Avoid ripping Criterion discs, which may include protected additions and copy protection.
Is the 1998 remake also public domain?
No. The 1998 remake is a separate work, made after its producer negotiated remake rights from Herk Harvey and John Clifford.
